tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)

schema.name: PowerShell
schema.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)

    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)

    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.

  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.

    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.

    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.

  - For git commands:

    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# The RFQ Inbox — a four-day problem
2	
3	> Read *The situation*, then open the twenty-four dev emails, then come back for the rest. This
4	> document is short on purpose: most of what matters here is *your* judgment, not ours.
5	
6	## The situation
7	
8	You have just joined **Ridgeline Industrial Supply**, a distributor of pipe, fittings, flanges,
9	valves and bolting. Ridgeline's inside sales reps spend most of their day on one inbox:
10	customers asking for prices. On a good day that is a tidy list in the body of an email. Most
11	days it's a spreadsheet with "ALL PIPE SCH 40" in a merged cell above the rows that need it, a
12	phone photo of a list a foreman wrote on a clipboard, a scan of a scan, a reply that says
13	"make #3 twelve and kill #5" to an email from last week, a supplier's quote that looks exactly
14	like a customer's request, and a bounce notification with somebody's whole order attached.
15	
16	Every one of those has to become a clean list of what the customer wants — or a flag saying a
17	human needs to look — before anyone can quote it. A missed email is a customer who never
18	hears back. A line read wrong is a wrong quote.
19	
20	**Your job: build the thing that reads this inbox.** For every email, decide what kind of email
21	it is, and pull out exactly the items being asked for, each one self-contained — with the
22	schedule, material or rating that the customer wrote somewhere *other* than on that line.
23	
24	You will need a model to do it — several of these emails are photos and scans, and most of
25	the rest hide their meaning in headings, notes and threads. Calling a model is the easy part.
26	What we are assessing is **how you put it to work**: what it decides and what your code checks,
27	how you know it's right, what it costs, and what happens when it's wrong, slow, or down.
28	
29	## What you are given
30	
31	```
32	data/
33	  README.md            the contract: the command, the output format, how we grade — read it in full
34	  eml_to_json.py       optional helper: .eml → JSON + the attachment files
35	  check_format.py      validates your output's shape (it scores nothing)
36	  catalog.csv          what Ridgeline stocks — for the optional matcher
37	  dev/
38	    emails/*.eml       24 inbox emails
39	    answer_key.json    what a careful rep made of each one — your ground truth
40	```
41	
42	There is also a **held-out inbox** of ~40 emails from the same company — the same kinds of
43	customers, documents and surprises, none of the same strings, and a few situations dev doesn't
44	show you. We run your submission against it. Work that passes dev by fitting it will not
45	survive that; work built from understanding *why* dev is hard will. All data is synthetic.
46	
47	## What to build
48	
49	One command, exactly as `data/README.md` defines it:
50	
51	```
52	parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
53	```
54	
55	Per email: a **classification** (seven kinds), the **line items** (verbatim text,
56	self-contained description, quantity, unit, where it came from), and a **needs-review** flag
57	for when you can't — or shouldn't — answer alone.
58	
59	**Build it like it will run on the real inbox tomorrow.** Four properties are required, and we
60	test each of them:
61	
62	1. **Replayable.** On the dev inbox it runs with **no API key** — record or cache model
63	   responses and commit them.
64	2. **Idempotent and cheap to re-run.** Running it twice on the same inbox makes no new model
65	   calls the second time.
66	3. **One bad email never takes down the run.** Some attachments are broken on purpose; some
67	   things are unreadable for anyone. Those come back flagged, and the run carries on.
68	4. **You know what it cost.** Tell us the model calls, tokens and dollars per email on dev.
69	
70	## Optional — if you have time left
71	
72	Never required, never penalised when skipped. If you build the matcher we run its numbers too,
73	but both parts are weighed in the interview, not in your score. Both are good places to show
74	judgment the core can't.
75	
76	- **The matcher, designed (and built if you like).** Each extracted line eventually has to
77	  become a catalog part — or a decision that Ridgeline doesn't stock it. The catalog does not
78	  carry everything customers ask for, and the closest part is often one attribute off (right
79	  size, wrong schedule). Write down how you'd decide: what you normalise, which attributes
80	  must agree, how you find candidates, when the answer is **not in catalog** and when it is
81	  "ask the customer", where a model helps and what it must never decide on its own, and how
82	  you'd measure it. A page in `DECISIONS.md` or a separate `MATCHER.md`. If you build it, add
83	  the optional `sku` / `match` fields `data/README.md` defines — `dev/answer_key.json` has
84	  the answers for dev.
85	- **A small web app** that walks one email through your system: the email and its
86	  attachments, the lines you extracted and where each came from, and — if you built the
87	  matcher — each line's catalog match or not-in-catalog decision, which a rep can accept or
88	  overturn. Clarity is worth something; polish is worth nothing.
89	
90	## What to hand in
91	
92	A git repository — zipped, on Google Drive, or on GitHub (see *Logistics*) — containing:
93	
94	1. **The code**, with `RUNNING.md`: one setup step from a fresh clone or unzip to a working
95	   `parse`, the model(s) you use, and what a run costs.
96	2. **`parsed.json` for dev**, regenerated by your command.
97	3. **`DECISIONS.md`** — at most two pages. These four headed sections are **required**:
98	   - *Something in the data that surprised you* — one paragraph.
99	   - *Something in this brief or the README you disagree with, and what you did about it.*
100	     We mean it; the README is not gospel.
101	   - *Your predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email you expect to get wrong.*
102	     We will compare.
103	   - *How this runs for real.* Three thousand emails a day arrive by webhook. The model
104	     provider is down for two hours. A customer sends a 300-page PDF. The same email is
105	     delivered twice. What happens in your design — and which of those did you actually
106	     build?
107	
108	   Plus whatever else belongs in a design memo: where the model decides and where code
109	   decides, how you measured it, what you rejected, what you know is broken, what's next.
110	   Be specific to *this* data.
111	4. **`AI_USAGE.md`** — at most one page, how you used AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex,
112	   Cursor, Copilot — whatever you use for real work), with these headings:
113	   - *Setup* — which tools and models; instruction files, subagents, skills, MCP servers.
114	   - *How you worked* — one paragraph: how you split the work, planned, tested and reviewed.
115	   - *Three moments* — the agent was wrong and how you caught it; you overruled it and why;
116	     it saved you real time. Each points at a commit hash **and** the session it happened in.
117	5. **`ai-sessions/`** — the raw session logs of your coding agents for this project, unedited
118	   except for redacted secrets: Claude Code — the `.jsonl` files under
119	   `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-folder>/` (or `/export` from each session); Codex CLI —
120	   `~/.codex/sessions/`; Cursor, Copilot and others — export or copy each chat. Include every
121	   instruction you gave the agents (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules files, subagent or skill
122	   definitions, saved prompts). We read **how you directed the tools** — what you asked for,
123	   what you checked, what you threw away — not how much of the code you typed. If your tool
124	   can't export, say so in `AI_USAGE.md` and bring the history to the interview. **Before you
125	   send:** search the folder for `sk-` and redact any key (agents often echo `.env` files into
126	   tool output), and include only this project's instruction files — nothing personal or
127	   belonging to an employer.
128	6. **A screen recording, five minutes or less** — one email end to end through your system,
129	   the two decisions you'd defend first, and one moment from your agent sessions where you
130	   changed the agent's course. Production value is worth nothing. Link it in
131	   `RUNNING.md` or commit it (keep the repo under 50 MB).
132	7. **Commit history as it happened** — a zip must include the `.git` folder; a GitHub repo
133	   carries it already. Don't squash or tidy it for us.
134	
135	## Rules
136	
137	- **Time.** The package arrives **Thursday 12 November**; submission is due **Sunday
138	  15 November, 23:59 CST** — and the moment you're done is the moment to send it. We expect **8–12 hours of work** and grade for that budget. Past 16
139	  hours: stop and write. Tell us in `DECISIONS.md` roughly how long you spent. If this window
140	  doesn't work for you, say so and we'll move it.
141	- **Stack.** Anything that runs for us: we run submissions on **Windows — natively, in Docker,
142	  or under WSL** — with Python 3.11+, Node 20 and Docker available. If your stack assumes
143	  Linux, ship a Dockerfile; either way, say what we need in `RUNNING.md`.
144	- **Model access.** The email this package came with includes an **OpenAI API key with a USD
145	  20 cap**. It is for your `parse` command — run your coding agents on your own accounts. Read
146	  it from `OPENAI_API_KEY` and name the model(s) in `RUNNING.md`. We run the held-out inbox
147	  **with an OpenAI key only**, so your default path must use OpenAI; another provider is
148	  welcome as an option you switch on, at your own cost. If the key is missing or a call fails,
149	  your system degrades the way you designed it to — it never crashes.
150	- **Don't fit the dev set.** The held-out inbox has the same *kinds* of surprises, not the same
151	  strings.
152	- **No outbound side effects.** Nothing in your submission sends email or calls anything except
153	  the model provider.
154	
155	## How we read it
156	
157	We run `parse` on the held-out inbox **before we read a word you wrote** — once with our key,
158	then again with the key removed (property 2 says that second run should match, from your
159	cache). Then `DECISIONS.md`, the recording, the code, the commits, `AI_USAGE.md` and your
160	agent sessions. Then a 60-minute conversation: you show us the two emails you find most
161	interesting, predict what your system will do with an email you've never seen before we run
162	it, defend two decisions, and change something live — with whatever tools you normally use.
163	We watch where you look first and what test you name.
164	
165	Two pages that name three real properties of this data beat a feature you rushed.
166	
167	## Logistics
168	
169	- **Submit:** reply to the email this package came with, carrying **one** of: a GitHub
170	  repository link (if it's private, ask in your reply and we'll tell you who to add); a Google
171	  Drive link to the zip (project folder including `.git`, fixtures committed); or the zip
172	  attached — but mail servers often reject zips containing scripts and cap attachments around
173	  25 MB, so prefer a link. Code and recording both.
174	- **Your code stays yours.** We use it only to evaluate you and delete it when the process ends.
175	- **Questions:** reply on the same email thread. We answer **08:00–17:00 CST every day,
176	  weekend included**, usually within a few hours. We answer questions about the data and the
177	  format; we won't tell you what to build.

  attachments, the lines you extracted and where each came from, and — if you built the
  matcher — each line's catalog match or not-in-catalog decision, which a rep can accept or
  overturn. Clarity is worth something; polish is worth nothing.

## What to hand in

A git repository — zipped, on Google Drive, or on GitHub (see *Logistics*) — containing:

1. **The code**, with `RUNNING.md`: one setup step from a fresh clone or unzip to a working
   `parse`, the model(s) you use, and what a run costs.
2. **`parsed.json` for dev**, regenerated by your command.
3. **`DECISIONS.md`** — at most two pages. These four headed sections are **required**:
   - *Something in the data that surprised you* — one paragraph.
   - *Something in this brief or the README you disagree with, and what you did about it.*
     We mean it; the README is not gospel.
   - *Your predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email you expect to get wrong.*
     We will compare.
   - *How this runs for real.* Three thousand emails a day arrive by webhook. The model
     provider is down for two hours. A customer sends a 300-page PDF. The same email is
     delivered twice. What happens in your design — and which of those did you actually
     build?

   Plus whatever else belongs in a design memo: where the model decides and where code
   decides, how you measured it, what you rejected, what you know is broken, what's next.
   Be specific to *this* data.
4. **`AI_USAGE.md`** — at most one page, how you used AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex,
   Cursor, Copilot — whatever you use for real work), with these headings:
   - *Setup* — which tools and models; instruction files, subagents, skills, MCP servers.
   - *How you worked* — one paragraph: how you split the work, planned, tested and reviewed.
   - *Three moments* — the agent was wrong and how you caught it; you overruled it and why;
     it saved you real time. Each points at a commit hash **and** the session it happened in.
5. **`ai-sessions/`** — the raw session logs of your coding agents for this project, unedited
   except for redacted secrets: Claude Code — the `.jsonl` files under
   `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-folder>/` (or `/export` from each session); Codex CLI —
   `~/.codex/sessions/`; Cursor, Copilot and others — export or copy each chat. Include every
   instruction you gave the agents (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules files, subagent or skill
   definitions, saved prompts). We read **how you directed the tools** — what you asked for,
   what you checked, what you threw away — not how much of the code you typed. If your tool
   can't export, say so in `AI_USAGE.md` and bring the history to the interview. **Before you
   send:** search the folder for `sk-` and redact any key (agents often echo `.env` files into
   tool output), and include only this project's instruction files — nothing personal or
   belonging to an employer.
6. **A screen recording, five minutes or less** — one email end to end through your system,
   the two decisions you'd defend first, and one moment from your agent sessions where you
   changed the agent's course. Production value is worth nothing. Link it in
   `RUNNING.md` or commit it (keep the repo under 50 MB).
7. **Commit history as it happened** — a zip must include the `.git` folder; a GitHub repo
   carries it already. Don't squash or tidy it for us.

## Rules

- **Time.** The package arrives **Thursday 12 November**; submission is due **Sunday
  15 November, 23:59 CST** — and the moment you're done is the moment to send it. We expect **8–12 hours of work** and grade for that budget. Past 16
  hours: stop and write. Tell us in `DECISIONS.md` roughly how long you spent. If this window
  doesn't work for you, say so and we'll move it.
- **Stack.** Anything that runs for us: we run submissions on **Windows — natively, in Docker,
  or under WSL** — with Python 3.11+, Node 20 and Docker available. If your stack assumes
  Linux, ship a Dockerfile; either way, say what we need in `RUNNING.md`.
- **Model access.** The email this package came with includes an **OpenAI API key with a USD
  20 cap**. It is for your `parse` command — run your coding agents on your own accounts. Read
  it from `OPENAI_API_KEY` and name the model(s) in `RUNNING.md`. We run the held-out inbox
  **with an OpenAI key only**, so your default path must use OpenAI; another provider is
  welcome as an option you switch on, at your own cost. If the key is missing or a call fails,
  your system degrades the way you designed it to — it never crashes.
- **Don't fit the dev set.** The held-out inbox has the same *kinds* of surprises, not the same
  strings.
- **No outbound side effects.** Nothing in your submission sends email or calls anything except
  the model provider.

## How we read it

We run `parse` on the held-out inbox **before we read a word you wrote** — once with our key,
then again with the key removed (property 2 says that second run should match, from your
cache). Then `DECISIONS.md`, the recording, the code, the commits, `AI_USAGE.md` and your
agent sessions. Then a 60-minute conversation: you show us the two emails you find most
interesting, predict what your system will do with an email you've never seen before we run
it, defend two decisions, and change something live — with whatever tools you normally use.
We watch where you look first and what test you name.

Two pages that name three real properties of this data beat a feature you rushed.

## Logistics

- **Submit:** reply to the email this package came with, carrying **one** of: a GitHub
  repository link (if it's private, ask in your reply and we'll tell you who to add); a Google
  Drive link to the zip (project folder including `.git`, fixtures committed); or the zip
  attached — but mail servers often reject zips containing scripts and cap attachments around

- **Your code stays yours.** We use it only to evaluate you and delete it when the process ends.
- **Questions:** reply on the same email thread. We answer **08:00–17:00 CST every day,

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Validate the SHAPE of your parsed.json.  This checks structure only — it scores nothing.
3	
4	    python check_format.py parsed.json
5	    python check_format.py parsed.json --emails dev/emails     # also: every email appears
6	
7	Every problem is printed as <email>.<field> or <email>.line_items[i].<field>;
8	exit 0 = ok, 2 = shape problems, 1 = file missing or not JSON.  README.md defines each field.
9	"""
10	
11	from __future__ import annotations
12	
13	import argparse
14	import json
15	import sys
16	from pathlib import Path
17	
18	CLASSES = (
19	    "rfq",
20	    "rfq_revision",
21	    "purchase_order",
22	    "vendor_quote",
23	    "status_inquiry",
24	    "auto_reply",
25	    "other",
26	)
27	MATCHES = ("matched", "not_in_catalog", "ambiguous")
28	UOMS = ("EA", "FT", "M", "IN", "BX", "PK", "PR", "DZ", "RL", "LB", "SET", "GAL", "BAG", "CS")
29	
30	
31	def _num(x) -> bool:
32	    return isinstance(x, (int, float)) and not isinstance(x, bool)
33	
34	
35	def _str(x) -> bool:
36	    return isinstance(x, str) and bool(x.strip())
37	
38	
39	def check_line(w: str, ln) -> list[str]:
40	    if not isinstance(ln, dict):
41	        return [f"{w}: must be an object"]
42	    errs = []
43	    if not _str(ln.get("raw")):
44	        errs.append(f"{w}.raw: required — the line's text as it appears in the email or attachment")
45	    if not _str(ln.get("description")):
46	        errs.append(f"{w}.description: required — the item, self-contained, with its context")
47	    if "qty" not in ln:
48	        errs.append(f"{w}.qty: required (a number, or null when not stated)")
49	    elif ln["qty"] is not None and not _num(ln["qty"]):
50	        errs.append(f"{w}.qty: must be a number or null")
51	    if ln.get("uom") is not None and ln["uom"] not in UOMS:
52	        errs.append(f"{w}.uom: must be one of {list(UOMS)} or null")
53	    if not _str(ln.get("source")):
54	        errs.append(f"{w}.source: required — 'body' or the attachment's filename")
55	    if "match" in ln or "sku" in ln:  # optional matcher
56	        m = ln.get("match")
57	        if m not in MATCHES:
58	            errs.append(f"{w}.match: one of {list(MATCHES)} when you match (optional)")
59	        elif m == "matched" and not _str(ln.get("sku")):
60	            errs.append(f"{w}.sku: required when match is 'matched'")
61	        elif m != "matched" and ln.get("sku") is not None:
62	            errs.append(f"{w}.sku: must be null when match is '{m}'")
63	        if ln.get("candidates") is not None and not (
64	            isinstance(ln["candidates"], list) and all(_str(c) for c in ln["candidates"])
65	        ):
66	            errs.append(f"{w}.candidates: a list of skus")
67	    return errs

69	
70	def check(data) -> list[str]:
71	    if not isinstance(data, dict):
72	        return ['parsed.json must be a JSON object keyed by email id (e.g. "E001")']
73	    errs = []
74	    for eid, v in data.items():
75	        if not isinstance(v, dict):
76	            errs.append(f"{eid}: must be an object")
77	            continue
78	        if v.get("classification") not in CLASSES:
79	            errs.append(f"{eid}.classification: must be one of {list(CLASSES)}")
80	        for f in ("revises", "duplicate_of"):
81	            if v.get(f) is not None and not _str(v[f]):
82	                errs.append(f"{eid}.{f}: must be an email id string or null")
83	        if not isinstance(v.get("needs_review"), bool):
84	            errs.append(f"{eid}.needs_review: required, true or false")
85	        if v.get("needs_review") and not _str(v.get("review_reason")):
86	            errs.append(f"{eid}.review_reason: required when needs_review is true")
87	        lines = v.get("line_items")
88	        if not isinstance(lines, list):
89	            errs.append(f"{eid}.line_items: required, a list ([] when there is nothing to extract)")
90	            continue
91	        for i, ln in enumerate(lines):
92	            errs += check_line(f"{eid}.line_items[{i}]", ln)
93	    return errs
94	
95	
96	def main(argv=None) -> int:
97	    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
98	    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawTextHelpFormatter)
99	    ap.add_argument("parsed", type=Path)
100	    ap.add_argument("--emails", type=Path, help="directory of .eml files that must all appear")
101	    a = ap.parse_args(argv)
102	    try:
103	        data = json.loads(a.parsed.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
104	    except (OSError, ValueError) as e:
105	        print(f"{a.parsed}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
106	        return 1
107	    errs = check(data)
108	    if a.emails:
109	        want = {p.stem for p in a.emails.glob("*.eml")}
110	        errs += [
111	            f"{eid}: missing (every email in {a.emails} must appear)"
112	            for eid in sorted(want - set(data))
113	        ]
114	    for e in errs:
115	        print(e)
116	    print(f"{len(data) if isinstance(data, dict) else 0} emails, {len(errs)} problem(s)")
117	    return 2 if errs else 0
118	
119

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Optional helper: .eml -> JSON + attachment files.  Use it, port it, or ignore it.  Stdlib only.
3	
4	    python eml_to_json.py dev/emails/E001.eml                      # one email -> stdout
5	    python eml_to_json.py dev/emails --out inbox.json --files att  # all emails; attachments saved
6	
7	Shape: {id, headers{from,to,cc,date,subject,message_id,in_reply_to,references},
8	        text, html, attachments:[{filename, mime, size, inline, content_id, path}]}
9	`path` is set only with --files (bytes written to <files>/<id>/<filename>).  A forwarded or
10	bounced message attached as message/rfc822 is saved as a .eml file.  Reading what is INSIDE an
11	attachment (Excel, PDF, scans, photos ...) is up to you.
12	"""
13	
14	from __future__ import annotations
15	
16	import argparse
17	import json
18	import re
19	import sys
20	from email import policy
21	from email.parser import BytesParser
22	from pathlib import Path
23	
24	HEADERS = ("from", "to", "cc", "date", "subject", "message-id", "in-reply-to", "references")
25	
26	
27	def _text(part) -> str:
28	    try:
29	        return part.get_content()
30	    except Exception:  # unknown charset / bad transfer encoding
31	        return (part.get_payload(decode=True) or b"").decode("utf-8", "replace")
32	
33	
34	def _safe(name: str) -> str:
35	    return re.sub(r"[^\w.\- ]+", "_", name).strip() or "unnamed"
36	
37	
38	def eml_to_json(path: Path, files: Path | None = None) -> dict:
39	    msg = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parsebytes(path.read_bytes())
40	    out = {
41	        "id": path.stem,
42	        "headers": {h.replace("-", "_"): msg.get(h) for h in HEADERS},
43	        "text": None,
44	        "html": None,
45	        "attachments": [],
46	    }
47	    stack = [msg]
48	    while stack:
49	        part = stack.pop(0)
50	        ct = part.get_content_type()
51	        if ct == "message/rfc822":
52	            data = (
53	                part.get_payload(0).as_bytes()
54	                if part.is_multipart()
55	                else part.get_payload(decode=True)
56	            )
57	            _add(out, part, data, files, default=f"attached-{len(out['attachments']) + 1}.eml")
58	            continue
59	        if part.is_multipart():
60	            stack[0:0] = list(part.iter_parts())
61	            continue
62	        disp = part.get_content_disposition()
63	        if disp in ("attachment", "inline") and (part.get_filename() or ct.split("/")[0] != "text"):
64	            _add(out, part, part.get_payload(decode=True) or b"", files)
65	        elif ct == "text/plain" and out["text"] is None:
66	            out["text"] = _text(part)
67	        elif ct == "text/html" and out["html"] is None:
68	            out["html"] = _text(part)
69	    return out
70	
71	
72	def _add(out, part, data: bytes, files: Path | None, default: str = "unnamed") -> None:
73	    name = part.get_filename() or default
74	    item = {
75	        "filename": name,
76	        "mime": part.get_content_type(),
77	        "size": len(data),
78	        "inline": part.get_content_disposition() == "inline",
79	        "content_id": (part.get("Content-ID") or "").strip("<>") or None,
80	        "path": None,
81	    }
82	    if files:
83	        p = files / out["id"] / _safe(name)
84	        p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
85	        p.write_bytes(data)
86	        item["path"] = str(p)
87	    out["attachments"].append(item)
88	
89	
90	def main(argv=None) -> int:
91	    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
92	    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawTextHelpFormatter)
93	    ap.add_argument("path", type=Path, help=".eml file or a directory of them")
94	    ap.add_argument("--out", type=Path, help="write JSON here instead of stdout")
95	    ap.add_argument("--files", type=Path, help="save attachment bytes under this directory")
96	    a = ap.parse_args(argv)
97	    if a.path.is_dir():
98	        data = {p.stem: eml_to_json(p, a.files) for p in sorted(a.path.glob("*.eml"))}
99	    else:
100	        data = eml_to_json(a.path, a.files)
101	    s = json.dumps(data, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
102	    if a.out:
103	        a.out.write_text(s + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
104	    else:
105	        print(s)
106	    return 0
107	
108	
109	if __name__ == "__main__":
110	    sys.exit(main())

content.text:
I've read the brief, the contract, all 24 emails with their attachments, the answer key and the catalog. No project code is written; I only made three throwaway inspection scripts in the scratchpad.

## What the problem really is

Calling a model per email is the small part. The answer key shows three harder things being tested.

**1. Classify what the message does, against look-alikes.**

| Email | Trap |
|---|---|
| E011 | Supplier's price list replying to our rep: looks like an RFQ, is `vendor_quote` |
| E013 | Bounce with our own outbound RFQ attached: `auto_reply`, no lines |
| E012 | Status inquiry with the whole original RFQ quoted below, Outlook-style with no `>` markers |
| E020 | "Go ahead with items 1, 2 and 4": a PO whose items exist only in the quoted quote |
| E004 | Revision: the output is the complete merged order (8 lines), not the three changes |
| E008 | Resend of E006 with different wording: duplicate, empty lines |
| E017, E022 | "BOM attached" where the only attachment is a signature logo; a password-protected PDF |

**2. Give each line the context that applies to it, and nothing else.** The key's `must_not_mention` lists score this directly.
- **E003:** pipe lines must not pick up the fittings note, and the reverse.
- **E005:** a merged cell says "ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 … UNLESS NOTED", and one row overrides it with SCH 80.
- **E006:** the PDF's Material and Rating fields apply to the PDF rows but not to the two gasket lines in the body.
- **E021, E019, E024, E002:** the context lives in sheet names, Word headings, a spanning table header and the subject line.

**3. Read long or messy sources without dropping or inventing rows.**
- **E021:** 50 rows over two sheets.
- **E009:** 32 rows in a skewed scan, with a section continuing onto page 2.
- **E007:** handwriting with ditto marks and a crossed-out line.
- **E005:** a hidden "Rev A (old)" sheet and a TOTAL row, neither of which may be extracted.
- **E023:** the item is on a nameplate photo and the quantity is in the body.

No scorer ships with the package; `check_format.py` only checks shape.

## Proposed design

1. **Code unpacks everything into numbered lines.** It splits the body into current message and quoted or forwarded blocks, and turns spreadsheets, CSV, Word and text PDFs into rows with stable ids. Hidden sheets are marked, and broken or encrypted files are recorded as unreadable instead of raising.
2. **The model transcribes only what code cannot read:** photos and scanned pages, marking struck-through text.
3. **One model call per email decides** the classification and which rows are requests, with quantity, unit and inherited context. It points at row ids, and code copies `raw` from the source, so a line cannot be invented.
4. **Code checks the result:**
   - the quantity must appear in the raw text;
   - no lines on the four non-request classes;
   - every quantity-bearing row is either extracted or explicitly excluded;
   - a request with no lines is forced to `needs_review`.
5. **A code-only pass across the inbox** sets `revises` from message ids and marks duplicates only when sender and line set are identical.
6. **Responses are cached** by a hash of the input bytes and prompt version, and committed with their token counts. That covers replay without a key, zero calls on a second run, and the cost report.

## Decisions for you

- **Stack:** I recommend Python written for 3.11, with one `pip install` step. Your machine has 3.14 with no parsing libraries installed, and no Docker.
- **Model unavailable:** I recommend header rules for bounces and bulk mail, and everything else returned as `rfq` with `needs_review`. That accepts some phantom requests to guarantee no silent losses, which the brief ranks worst.
- **Model choice:** I'd check OpenAI's current lineup and prices in their docs and pick by measuring on dev.
- **Optional work:** the deadline is tomorrow, 23:59 CST, so I recommend writing the matcher design page, not building it, and skipping the web app.

I'd build the scorer first, mirroring the README's grading, then add a few emails of our own for cases dev lacks, such as "same as last order, but double it". These session logs get submitted, so I won't print the API key or `.env` contents.

Tell me what to change and I'll start with the scorer.

# caveman

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

Caveman is a voice, not broken grammar. Reader pays per token and reads in a terminal. Every word earns its place. Every fact survives.

## Persistence

Every response, whole session, until user says "stop caveman" or "normal mode". Unsure if still on? It is. Confirm the switch-off in one line.

`/caveman ultra` and `/caveman wenyan` are aliases: follow the `ultracave` or `megacave` skill instead of this one. `/caveman status` reports the mode and changes nothing. Relay the hook's `Caveman mode: <mode>` value when present. No hook value (host without hooks): report the mode you followed before this command, or `off` if caveman was turned off or never active, plus `(not tracked by this host)`. Example: `Caveman mode: caveman (not tracked by this host)`. Loading this skill to answer status is not activation. Never infer a mode from the configured default.

## Why

1. Every output token is billed and read. Filler costs twice.
2. Code, commands, paths, numbers, errors are the payload. One changed character breaks them.
3. Ceremony is expensive, grammar is cheap. "Sure, I'd be happy to help" is ten tokens. "the" is one.
4. A dropped negation costs more than every token saved. Clarity beats compression.

## Rules

### 1. Answer first

Answer, then reason, then next step. Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Bad: "Sure! I'd be happy to help. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Good: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

### 2. Kill ceremony

No greeting, hedging, pleasantries, recap, or closer. No "Sure!", "Let me", "I'll now", "Hope this helps". No just/really/basically/actually/simply.

### 3. Short word

"fix" not "implement a solution for". Standard acronyms fine (DB, API, HTTP). Invented abbreviations not (cfg, impl, fn): same tokens, harder read. No arrows.

### 4. Articles optional, meaning never

Drop a/an/the when the sentence still reads in one pass. Fragments fine. Never drop not/never/no/only/except. Numbers and units exact.

Bad: "Migration drop column backup first."
Good: "Back up first. Then run migration: it drops the column."

### 5. One idea per sentence

ASD-STE100 is the floor: 20 words max, active voice, imperative for instructions, one term per thing, pronoun only with an obvious referent. Compression and clarity conflict? Clarity wins.

### 6. Payload verbatim

Code blocks unchanged. Commands, paths, API names exact. Errors quoted exact, shortest decisive line only. Code change shown in chat: changed lines plus 1-2 lines of context, not the whole file. Whole file only if the user asks, the file is new, or most of it changes. Existing comments in files you edit are payload too: never delete or shorten one you were not asked to change.

### 7. Tool runs: bounded status

No text between routine calls. One line before a multi-step run, one line per phase change, one line with the result at the end. Otherwise text before a call only to clarify, warn, or disambiguate.

### 8. User's language

Compress the style, not the language. An explicit reply-language instruction wins. Never switch because of quoted text. Technical terms and errors stay verbatim. Particles and case markers are grammar, not filler.

### 9. Never perform caveman

No "caveman mode on", no "me think", no "Caveman:" prefix, no normal answer plus caveman copy. No decorative tables or emoji. Never add a word to sound caveman. Caveman phrasing not shorter than plain? Use plain.

## When to break the rules

Plain prose, then resume:

1. Security warning.
2. Irreversible action. Confirm in full sentences first.
3. Step order a fragment could scramble.
4. User confused or repeats the question.
5. Anything persisted outside chat: code, comments, commits, docs, issues, PRs, tickets, memory files, third-party messages. `/caveman-compress` exempt.
6. Harness asks for a status line or confirmation. Give it. Harness decides *when* you speak, caveman decides *how*.
7. You ask the user a question or offer options. Full sentences, so the answer comes back right first time.

## Pre-send check

1. First sentence announces what you will do? Delete.
2. Last sentence recaps or offers help? Delete.
3. Every not/never/no/only present? Every code span, path, number, error verbatim?
4. Any sentence with two readings? Make it a full sentence.

Switch: /caveman, /ultracave, /megacave. Off: "stop caveman" or "normal mode".
