tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.text:

content.content:
1	# The RFQ Inbox — a four-day problem
2	
3	> Read *The situation*, then open the twenty-four dev emails, then come back for the rest. This
4	> document is short on purpose: most of what matters here is *your* judgment, not ours.
5	
6	## The situation
7	
8	You have just joined **Ridgeline Industrial Supply**, a distributor of pipe, fittings, flanges,
9	valves and bolting. Ridgeline's inside sales reps spend most of their day on one inbox:
10	customers asking for prices. On a good day that is a tidy list in the body of an email. Most
11	days it's a spreadsheet with "ALL PIPE SCH 40" in a merged cell above the rows that need it, a
12	phone photo of a list a foreman wrote on a clipboard, a scan of a scan, a reply that says
13	"make #3 twelve and kill #5" to an email from last week, a supplier's quote that looks exactly
14	like a customer's request, and a bounce notification with somebody's whole order attached.
15	
16	Every one of those has to become a clean list of what the customer wants — or a flag saying a
17	human needs to look — before anyone can quote it. A missed email is a customer who never
18	hears back. A line read wrong is a wrong quote.
19	
20	**Your job: build the thing that reads this inbox.** For every email, decide what kind of email
21	it is, and pull out exactly the items being asked for, each one self-contained — with the
22	schedule, material or rating that the customer wrote somewhere *other* than on that line.
23	
24	You will need a model to do it — several of these emails are photos and scans, and most of
25	the rest hide their meaning in headings, notes and threads. Calling a model is the easy part.
26	What we are assessing is **how you put it to work**: what it decides and what your code checks,
27	how you know it's right, what it costs, and what happens when it's wrong, slow, or down.
28	
29	## What you are given
30	
31	```
32	data/
33	  README.md            the contract: the command, the output format, how we grade — read it in full
34	  eml_to_json.py       optional helper: .eml → JSON + the attachment files
35	  check_format.py      validates your output's shape (it scores nothing)
36	  catalog.csv          what Ridgeline stocks — for the optional matcher
37	  dev/
38	    emails/*.eml       24 inbox emails
39	    answer_key.json    what a careful rep made of each one — your ground truth
40	```
41	
42	There is also a **held-out inbox** of ~40 emails from the same company — the same kinds of
43	customers, documents and surprises, none of the same strings, and a few situations dev doesn't
44	show you. We run your submission against it. Work that passes dev by fitting it will not
45	survive that; work built from understanding *why* dev is hard will. All data is synthetic.
46	
47	## What to build
48	
49	One command, exactly as `data/README.md` defines it:
50	
51	```
52	parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
53	```
54	
55	Per email: a **classification** (seven kinds), the **line items** (verbatim text,
56	self-contained description, quantity, unit, where it came from), and a **needs-review** flag
57	for when you can't — or shouldn't — answer alone.
58	
59	**Build it like it will run on the real inbox tomorrow.** Four properties are required, and we
60	test each of them:
61	
62	1. **Replayable.** On the dev inbox it runs with **no API key** — record or cache model
63	   responses and commit them.
64	2. **Idempotent and cheap to re-run.** Running it twice on the same inbox makes no new model
65	   calls the second time.
66	3. **One bad email never takes down the run.** Some attachments are broken on purpose; some
67	   things are unreadable for anyone. Those come back flagged, and the run carries on.
68	4. **You know what it cost.** Tell us the model calls, tokens and dollars per email on dev.
69	
70	## Optional — if you have time left
71	
72	Never required, never penalised when skipped. If you build the matcher we run its numbers too,
73	but both parts are weighed in the interview, not in your score. Both are good places to show
74	judgment the core can't.
75	
76	- **The matcher, designed (and built if you like).** Each extracted line eventually has to
77	  become a catalog part — or a decision that Ridgeline doesn't stock it. The catalog does not
78	  carry everything customers ask for, and the closest part is often one attribute off (right
79	  size, wrong schedule). Write down how you'd decide: what you normalise, which attributes
80	  must agree, how you find candidates, when the answer is **not in catalog** and when it is
81	  "ask the customer", where a model helps and what it must never decide on its own, and how
82	  you'd measure it. A page in `DECISIONS.md` or a separate `MATCHER.md`. If you build it, add
83	  the optional `sku` / `match` fields `data/README.md` defines — `dev/answer_key.json` has
84	  the answers for dev.
85	- **A small web app** that walks one email through your system: the email and its
86	  attachments, the lines you extracted and where each came from, and — if you built the
87	  matcher — each line's catalog match or not-in-catalog decision, which a rep can accept or
88	  overturn. Clarity is worth something; polish is worth nothing.
89	
90	## What to hand in
91	
92	A git repository — zipped, on Google Drive, or on GitHub (see *Logistics*) — containing:
93	
94	1. **The code**, with `RUNNING.md`: one setup step from a fresh clone or unzip to a working
95	   `parse`, the model(s) you use, and what a run costs.
96	2. **`parsed.json` for dev**, regenerated by your command.
97	3. **`DECISIONS.md`** — at most two pages. These four headed sections are **required**:
98	   - *Something in the data that surprised you* — one paragraph.
99	   - *Something in this brief or the README you disagree with, and what you did about it.*
100	     We mean it; the README is not gospel.
101	   - *Your predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email you expect to get wrong.*
102	     We will compare.
103	   - *How this runs for real.* Three thousand emails a day arrive by webhook. The model
104	     provider is down for two hours. A customer sends a 300-page PDF. The same email is
105	     delivered twice. What happens in your design — and which of those did you actually
106	     build?
107	
108	   Plus whatever else belongs in a design memo: where the model decides and where code
109	   decides, how you measured it, what you rejected, what you know is broken, what's next.
110	   Be specific to *this* data.
111	4. **`AI_USAGE.md`** — at most one page, how you used AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex,
112	   Cursor, Copilot — whatever you use for real work), with these headings:
113	   - *Setup* — which tools and models; instruction files, subagents, skills, MCP servers.
114	   - *How you worked* — one paragraph: how you split the work, planned, tested and reviewed.
115	   - *Three moments* — the agent was wrong and how you caught it; you overruled it and why;
116	     it saved you real time. Each points at a commit hash **and** the session it happened in.
117	5. **`ai-sessions/`** — the raw session logs of your coding agents for this project, unedited
118	   except for redacted secrets: Claude Code — the `.jsonl` files under
119	   `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-folder>/` (or `/export` from each session); Codex CLI —
120	   `~/.codex/sessions/`; Cursor, Copilot and others — export or copy each chat. Include every
121	   instruction you gave the agents (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules files, subagent or skill
122	   definitions, saved prompts). We read **how you directed the tools** — what you asked for,
123	   what you checked, what you threw away — not how much of the code you typed. If your tool
124	   can't export, say so in `AI_USAGE.md` and bring the history to the interview. **Before you
125	   send:** search the folder for `sk-` and redact any key (agents often echo `.env` files into
126	   tool output), and include only this project's instruction files — nothing personal or
127	   belonging to an employer.
128	6. **A screen recording, five minutes or less** — one email end to end through your system,
129	   the two decisions you'd defend first, and one moment from your agent sessions where you
130	   changed the agent's course. Production value is worth nothing. Link it in
131	   `RUNNING.md` or commit it (keep the repo under 50 MB).
132	7. **Commit history as it happened** — a zip must include the `.git` folder; a GitHub repo
133	   carries it already. Don't squash or tidy it for us.
134	
135	## Rules
136	
137	- **Time.** The package arrives **Thursday 12 November**; submission is due **Sunday
138	  15 November, 23:59 CST** — and the moment you're done is the moment to send it. We expect **8–12 hours of work** and grade for that budget. Past 16
139	  hours: stop and write. Tell us in `DECISIONS.md` roughly how long you spent. If this window
140	  doesn't work for you, say so and we'll move it.
141	- **Stack.** Anything that runs for us: we run submissions on **Windows — natively, in Docker,
142	  or under WSL** — with Python 3.11+, Node 20 and Docker available. If your stack assumes
143	  Linux, ship a Dockerfile; either way, say what we need in `RUNNING.md`.
144	- **Model access.** The email this package came with includes an **OpenAI API key with a USD
145	  20 cap**. It is for your `parse` command — run your coding agents on your own accounts. Read
146	  it from `OPENAI_API_KEY` and name the model(s) in `RUNNING.md`. We run the held-out inbox
147	  **with an OpenAI key only**, so your default path must use OpenAI; another provider is
148	  welcome as an option you switch on, at your own cost. If the key is missing or a call fails,
149	  your system degrades the way you designed it to — it never crashes.
150	- **Don't fit the dev set.** The held-out inbox has the same *kinds* of surprises, not the same
151	  strings.
152	- **No outbound side effects.** Nothing in your submission sends email or calls anything except
153	  the model provider.
154	
155	## How we read it
156	
157	We run `parse` on the held-out inbox **before we read a word you wrote** — once with our key,
158	then again with the key removed (property 2 says that second run should match, from your
159	cache). Then `DECISIONS.md`, the recording, the code, the commits, `AI_USAGE.md` and your
160	agent sessions. Then a 60-minute conversation: you show us the two emails you find most
161	interesting, predict what your system will do with an email you've never seen before we run
162	it, defend two decisions, and change something live — with whatever tools you normally use.
163	We watch where you look first and what test you name.
164	
165	Two pages that name three real properties of this data beat a feature you rushed.
166	
167	## Logistics
168	
169	- **Submit:** reply to the email this package came with, carrying **one** of: a GitHub
170	  repository link (if it's private, ask in your reply and we'll tell you who to add); a Google
171	  Drive link to the zip (project folder including `.git`, fixtures committed); or the zip
172	  attached — but mail servers often reject zips containing scripts and cap attachments around
173	  25 MB, so prefer a link. Code and recording both.
174	- **Your code stays yours.** We use it only to evaluate you and delete it when the process ends.
175	- **Questions:** reply on the same email thread. We answer **08:00–17:00 CST every day,
176	  weekend included**, usually within a few hours. We answer questions about the data and the
177	  format; we won't tell you what to build.

1	# data/ — the files, the contract, the grading
2	
3	```
4	dev/emails/*.eml       the inbox: 24 RFC-822 emails (E001.eml …) — plain text, HTML, Excel,
5	                       CSV, Word, text PDFs, scanned PDFs, phone photos, pasted screenshots, threads
6	dev/answer_key.json    what a careful inside sales rep (ISR) made of each email — your ground truth
7	check_format.py        validates the shape of your output (it scores nothing)
8	catalog.csv            what Ridgeline stocks — used only by the OPTIONAL matcher (see the end)
9	eml_to_json.py         optional: .eml → JSON + the attachment files. Use it, port it, or ignore it —
10	                       unpacking MIME is not what we grade; reading what is inside the attachments is.
11	```
12	
13	A **held-out inbox** from the same company — same kinds of customers, documents and surprises,
14	none of the same strings — is not shipped; your submission is run against it.
15	
16	## The command (this is how we run you, so the shape is mandatory)
17	
18	```
19	<your command> parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
20	```
21	
22	It reads every `.eml` in `<dir>` and writes one JSON file. Check it with
23	`python check_format.py parsed.json --emails <dir>` (exit 0 = shape ok).
24	
25	## parsed.json
26	
27	One object keyed by the `.eml` filename stem. **Every email in the directory must appear.**
28	
29	```json
30	{
31	  "E003": {
32	    "classification": "rfq",
33	    "revises": null,
34	    "duplicate_of": null,
35	    "needs_review": false,
36	    "review_reason": null,
37	    "line_items": [
38	      {
39	        "raw": "2\" x 21' - 12 lengths",
40	        "description": "2\" pipe, SCH 40 A53B ERW, threaded & coupled, 21' lengths",
41	        "qty": 12,
42	        "uom": "EA",
43	        "source": "body"
44	      }
45	    ]
46	  }
47	}
48	```
49	
50	### classification — exactly one per email
51	
52	| value | the **current** message … | line_items |
53	|---|---|---|
54	| `rfq` | asks us to price or check availability of items | the items |
55	| `rfq_revision` | changes a request made earlier in the same thread (quantities, additions, removals) | the **complete** order as now intended; `revises` = the earlier email's id if it is in the inbox, else null |
56	| `purchase_order` | commits to buy — a PO, "please process", "go ahead with items 1–3" | the items ordered |
57	| `vendor_quote` | is a supplier quoting or answering **us** | `[]` |
58	| `status_inquiry` | asks about an existing quote or order (update? ETA? tracking?) | `[]` |
59	| `auto_reply` | is machine-generated: out-of-office, bounce, receipt | `[]` |
60	| `other` | anything else: marketing, invoices and remittances, job applications, internal chatter, "we went with someone else" | `[]` |
61	
62	Classify what the current message *does* — not the subject line, not the quoted history.
63	
64	### line_items — one per thing the customer is asking for
65	
66	- **What counts.** Items in the current message, its attachments and pasted pictures, and —
67	  when one of our own reps forwards a customer's email — in the forwarded content. Not items
68	  in quoted earlier messages (they were handled when they arrived), not headings, notes,
69	  totals, prices, signatures, crossed-out lines, or old revisions of a document.
70	- **`raw`** — the line's text as it appears where you found it (a table row's cells on one
71	  line; for a picture or scan, your reading of it). We pair your lines with ours on these
72	  tokens, so keep it close to the source.
73	- **`description`** — the item **self-contained**, as an ISR would type it into a quote
74	  without re-reading the email: the line's own words plus every heading, note, column
75	  header, sheet name, form field, subject line or earlier line that applies to it — and
76	  nothing that doesn't apply to it. Never invent a spec the email doesn't give.
77	- **`qty` / `uom`** — as the customer stated it, not converted. A number spelled out is a
78	  number; a vague amount ("a couple", "enough for the job") is `null`. A size, schedule,
79	  length, rating, part number or price is never a quantity. `uom` is one of `EA FT M IN BX
80	  PK PR DZ RL LB SET GAL BAG CS`, or `null` when no unit is stated (we read `null` as `EA`).
81	- **`source`** — `"body"`, or the filename of the attachment / pasted image the line came from.
82	
83	### Threads, duplicates, forwards
84	
85	- A reply that changes an earlier request → `rfq_revision` with the **complete** order as the
86	  customer now intends it; the earlier email keeps its own lines as they were on arrival.
87	- The same request sent twice → **the email with the later `Date:` is the duplicate**: same
88	  classification as the original, `duplicate_of` = the original's id, `line_items: []`.
89	- Anything **from** `@ridgeline-supply.example` is one of our own reps, usually forwarding a
90	  customer's email; classify it as the customer's email, and read the rep's own note too.
91	
92	### needs_review — "a human has to look at this before anyone quotes it"
93	
94	`true` when the email asks for something you cannot fully read or resolve: the attachment it
95	points at is missing or can't be opened, or the items themselves are only identified by
96	something that isn't in the email ("same as our last order, but double it"). Put the reason in `review_reason` (required when `true`) and still
97	return whatever lines you *could* read. Only for `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`.
98	
99	## Optional: matching to the catalog
100	
101	If you build the optional matcher, add three fields to each line item:
102	
103	```json
104	{"raw": "...", "description": "...", "qty": 12, "uom": "EA", "source": "body",
105	 "sku": "RL-12345", "match": "matched", "match_reason": "2\" 150# RF weld neck A105: one part fits"}
106	```
107	
108	- `match` is one of `matched` (exactly one catalog part is what the customer asked for —
109	  `sku` is it), `not_in_catalog` (we don't stock it — `sku: null`), or `ambiguous` (more than
110	  one stocked part fits what the customer wrote and they'd have to choose — `sku: null`,
111	  optional `candidates: [skus]`).
112	- `match_reason` — one short line a rep can check.
113	- **Not in catalog is a decision, not a failure.** Ridgeline doesn't stock everything
114	  customers ask for, and the nearest catalog part is often one attribute away — right size and
115	  type, wrong schedule, rating or material. Quoting that part is a wrong quote.
116	- `catalog.csv` columns: `sku, description, category, product, size, spec` (schedule or
117	  pressure class)`, material, ends, extra, uom`. Descriptions are abbreviated the way an ERP
118	  prints them.
119	
120	## World facts
121	
122	- Ridgeline Industrial Supply sells pipe, fittings, flanges, valves, gaskets, bolting and
123	  related industrial supplies. The RFQ inbox is `rfq@ridgeline-supply.example`.
124	- Our quotes are numbered `Q-26-…`. Customers' RFQ and PO numbers are theirs.
125	- A supplier answering *our* request for pricing is a `vendor_quote`, however much it looks
126	  like a list of items.
127	
128	## What we grade
129	
130	Your `parse` command on the held-out inbox, against our key, **before we read anything you wrote**.
131	
132	**Headline numbers** — the expensive failures, in this order:
133	1. **Silent losses** — an email that needed someone to act (it has items, or needs review)
134	   came back with no lines and no review flag. That customer never hears back.
135	2. **Hallucinated lines** — lines that aren't requests: quoted history, headings, prices,
136	   signatures, crossed-out or superseded rows.
137	3. **Lost and phantom requests** — a request classified as something else (lost), or a
138	   vendor quote / bounce / newsletter classified as a request (phantom).
139	
140	Then: classification accuracy, line recall and precision, and on paired lines — `qty`,
141	`uom`, `source`, and **context carried** (does the `description` mention what the key's
142	`must_mention` lists, and none of its `must_not_mention`?). Plus `revises` / `duplicate_of`
143	links and `needs_review` precision/recall.
144	
145	**Optional matcher**, if present: confident wrong matches (you named a part; the answer was a
146	different part, *not in catalog*, or *ambiguous*), not-in-catalog recall, and match accuracy.
147	
148	**`answer_key.json` fields beyond the schema:** `id` (`<email>-<n>`); `qty_tol` (relative
149	tolerance on qty: `0` exact, `null` = unscored); `must_mention` (phrases the description must
150	contain; `"a|b"` = either; case, spaces and punctuation ignored, and common spellings of the
151	same spec count as equal — Sch/Schedule, 150#/150 lb/Class 150, BW/butt weld, threaded/NPT,
152	SMLS/seamless, galv/galvanized, and the catalog's abbreviations ELL, VLV, FLG, GSKT, SPW, MI,
153	CS, FP, RED, CPLG); `must_not_mention` (phrases
154	it must not contain — a default that this line overrides, or a note that belongs to another
155	section); `sku` / `match` / `candidates` (the catalog answer for the optional matcher).

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Validate the SHAPE of your parsed.json.  This checks structure only — it scores nothing.
3	
4	    python check_format.py parsed.json
5	    python check_format.py parsed.json --emails dev/emails     # also: every email appears
6	
7	Every problem is printed as <email>.<field> or <email>.line_items[i].<field>;
8	exit 0 = ok, 2 = shape problems, 1 = file missing or not JSON.  README.md defines each field.
9	"""
10	
11	from __future__ import annotations
12	
13	import argparse
14	import json
15	import sys
16	from pathlib import Path
17	
18	CLASSES = (
19	    "rfq",
20	    "rfq_revision",
21	    "purchase_order",
22	    "vendor_quote",
23	    "status_inquiry",
24	    "auto_reply",
25	    "other",
26	)
27	MATCHES = ("matched", "not_in_catalog", "ambiguous")
28	UOMS = ("EA", "FT", "M", "IN", "BX", "PK", "PR", "DZ", "RL", "LB", "SET", "GAL", "BAG", "CS")
29	
30	
31	def _num(x) -> bool:
32	    return isinstance(x, (int, float)) and not isinstance(x, bool)
33	
34	
35	def _str(x) -> bool:
36	    return isinstance(x, str) and bool(x.strip())
37	
38	
39	def check_line(w: str, ln) -> list[str]:
40	    if not isinstance(ln, dict):
41	        return [f"{w}: must be an object"]
42	    errs = []
43	    if not _str(ln.get("raw")):
44	        errs.append(f"{w}.raw: required — the line's text as it appears in the email or attachment")
45	    if not _str(ln.get("description")):
46	        errs.append(f"{w}.description: required — the item, self-contained, with its context")
47	    if "qty" not in ln:
48	        errs.append(f"{w}.qty: required (a number, or null when not stated)")
49	    elif ln["qty"] is not None and not _num(ln["qty"]):
50	        errs.append(f"{w}.qty: must be a number or null")
51	    if ln.get("uom") is not None and ln["uom"] not in UOMS:
52	        errs.append(f"{w}.uom: must be one of {list(UOMS)} or null")
53	    if not _str(ln.get("source")):
54	        errs.append(f"{w}.source: required — 'body' or the attachment's filename")
55	    if "match" in ln or "sku" in ln:  # optional matcher
56	        m = ln.get("match")
57	        if m not in MATCHES:
58	            errs.append(f"{w}.match: one of {list(MATCHES)} when you match (optional)")
59	        elif m == "matched" and not _str(ln.get("sku")):
60	            errs.append(f"{w}.sku: required when match is 'matched'")
61	        elif m != "matched" and ln.get("sku") is not None:
62	            errs.append(f"{w}.sku: must be null when match is '{m}'")
63	        if ln.get("candidates") is not None and not (
64	            isinstance(ln["candidates"], list) and all(_str(c) for c in ln["candidates"])
65	        ):
66	            errs.append(f"{w}.candidates: a list of skus")
67	    return errs
68	
69	
70	def check(data) -> list[str]:
71	    if not isinstance(data, dict):
72	        return ['parsed.json must be a JSON object keyed by email id (e.g. "E001")']
73	    errs = []
74	    for eid, v in data.items():
75	        if not isinstance(v, dict):
76	            errs.append(f"{eid}: must be an object")
77	            continue
78	        if v.get("classification") not in CLASSES:
79	            errs.append(f"{eid}.classification: must be one of {list(CLASSES)}")
80	        for f in ("revises", "duplicate_of"):
81	            if v.get(f) is not None and not _str(v[f]):
82	                errs.append(f"{eid}.{f}: must be an email id string or null")
83	        if not isinstance(v.get("needs_review"), bool):
84	            errs.append(f"{eid}.needs_review: required, true or false")
85	        if v.get("needs_review") and not _str(v.get("review_reason")):
86	            errs.append(f"{eid}.review_reason: required when needs_review is true")
87	        lines = v.get("line_items")
88	        if not isinstance(lines, list):
89	            errs.append(f"{eid}.line_items: required, a list ([] when there is nothing to extract)")
90	            continue
91	        for i, ln in enumerate(lines):
92	            errs += check_line(f"{eid}.line_items[{i}]", ln)
93	    return errs
94	
95	
96	def main(argv=None) -> int:
97	    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
98	    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawTextHelpFormatter)
99	    ap.add_argument("parsed", type=Path)
100	    ap.add_argument("--emails", type=Path, help="directory of .eml files that must all appear")
101	    a = ap.parse_args(argv)
102	    try:
103	        data = json.loads(a.parsed.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
104	    except (OSError, ValueError) as e:
105	        print(f"{a.parsed}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
106	        return 1
107	    errs = check(data)
108	    if a.emails:
109	        want = {p.stem for p in a.emails.glob("*.eml")}
110	        errs += [
111	            f"{eid}: missing (every email in {a.emails} must appear)"
112	            for eid in sorted(want - set(data))
113	        ]
114	    for e in errs:
115	        print(e)
116	    print(f"{len(data) if isinstance(data, dict) else 0} emails, {len(errs)} problem(s)")
117	    return 2 if errs else 0
118	
119	
120	if __name__ == "__main__":
121	    sys.exit(main())

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Optional helper: .eml -> JSON + attachment files.  Use it, port it, or ignore it.  Stdlib only.
3	
4	    python eml_to_json.py dev/emails/E001.eml                      # one email -> stdout
5	    python eml_to_json.py dev/emails --out inbox.json --files att  # all emails; attachments saved
6	
7	Shape: {id, headers{from,to,cc,date,subject,message_id,in_reply_to,references},
8	        text, html, attachments:[{filename, mime, size, inline, content_id, path}]}
9	`path` is set only with --files (bytes written to <files>/<id>/<filename>).  A forwarded or
10	bounced message attached as message/rfc822 is saved as a .eml file.  Reading what is INSIDE an
11	attachment (Excel, PDF, scans, photos ...) is up to you.
12	"""
13	
14	from __future__ import annotations
15	
16	import argparse
17	import json
18	import re
19	import sys
20	from email import policy
21	from email.parser import BytesParser
22	from pathlib import Path
23	
24	HEADERS = ("from", "to", "cc", "date", "subject", "message-id", "in-reply-to", "references")
25	
26	
27	def _text(part) -> str:
28	    try:
29	        return part.get_content()
30	    except Exception:  # unknown charset / bad transfer encoding
31	        return (part.get_payload(decode=True) or b"").decode("utf-8", "replace")
32	
33	
34	def _safe(name: str) -> str:
35	    return re.sub(r"[^\w.\- ]+", "_", name).strip() or "unnamed"
36	
37	
38	def eml_to_json(path: Path, files: Path | None = None) -> dict:
39	    msg = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parsebytes(path.read_bytes())
40	    out = {
41	        "id": path.stem,
42	        "headers": {h.replace("-", "_"): msg.get(h) for h in HEADERS},
43	        "text": None,
44	        "html": None,
45	        "attachments": [],
46	    }
47	    stack = [msg]
48	    while stack:
49	        part = stack.pop(0)
50	        ct = part.get_content_type()
51	        if ct == "message/rfc822":
52	            data = (
53	                part.get_payload(0).as_bytes()
54	                if part.is_multipart()
55	                else part.get_payload(decode=True)
56	            )
57	            _add(out, part, data, files, default=f"attached-{len(out['attachments']) + 1}.eml")
58	            continue
59	        if part.is_multipart():
60	            stack[0:0] = list(part.iter_parts())
61	            continue
62	        disp = part.get_content_disposition()
63	        if disp in ("attachment", "inline") and (part.get_filename() or ct.split("/")[0] != "text"):
64	            _add(out, part, part.get_payload(decode=True) or b"", files)
65	        elif ct == "text/plain" and out["text"] is None:
66	            out["text"] = _text(part)
67	        elif ct == "text/html" and out["html"] is None:
68	            out["html"] = _text(part)
69	    return out
70	
71	
72	def _add(out, part, data: bytes, files: Path | None, default: str = "unnamed") -> None:
73	    name = part.get_filename() or default
74	    item = {
75	        "filename": name,
76	        "mime": part.get_content_type(),
77	        "size": len(data),
78	        "inline": part.get_content_disposition() == "inline",
79	        "content_id": (part.get("Content-ID") or "").strip("<>") or None,
80	        "path": None,
81	    }
82	    if files:
83	        p = files / out["id"] / _safe(name)
84	        p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
85	        p.write_bytes(data)
86	        item["path"] = str(p)
87	    out["attachments"].append(item)
88	
89	
90	def main(argv=None) -> int:
91	    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
92	    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawTextHelpFormatter)
93	    ap.add_argument("path", type=Path, help=".eml file or a directory of them")
94	    ap.add_argument("--out", type=Path, help="write JSON here instead of stdout")
95	    ap.add_argument("--files", type=Path, help="save attachment bytes under this directory")
96	    a = ap.parse_args(argv)
97	    if a.path.is_dir():
98	        data = {p.stem: eml_to_json(p, a.files) for p in sorted(a.path.glob("*.eml"))}
99	    else:
100	        data = eml_to_json(a.path, a.files)
101	    s = json.dumps(data, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
102	    if a.out:
103	        a.out.write_text(s + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
104	    else:
105	        print(s)
106	    return 0
107	
108	
109	if __name__ == "__main__":
110	    sys.exit(main())

import re
import sys
import zipfile

sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
path = sys.argv[1]
want = sys.argv[2:]  # substrings of member names to print in full
z = zipfile.ZipFile(path)
print("##", path)
for i in z.infolist():
    print(f"  {i.file_size:>8}  {i.filename}")
for i in z.infolist():
    if any(w in i.filename for w in want) and i.filename.endswith((".xml", ".rels")):
        x = z.read(i).decode("utf-8", "replace")

# caveman

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

Caveman is a voice, not broken grammar. Reader pays per token and reads in a terminal. Every word earns its place. Every fact survives.

## Persistence

Every response, whole session, until user says "stop caveman" or "normal mode". Unsure if still on? It is. Confirm the switch-off in one line.

`/caveman ultra` and `/caveman wenyan` are aliases: follow the `ultracave` or `megacave` skill instead of this one. `/caveman status` reports the mode and changes nothing. Relay the hook's `Caveman mode: <mode>` value when present. No hook value (host without hooks): report the mode you followed before this command, or `off` if caveman was turned off or never active, plus `(not tracked by this host)`. Example: `Caveman mode: caveman (not tracked by this host)`. Loading this skill to answer status is not activation. Never infer a mode from the configured default.

## Why

1. Every output token is billed and read. Filler costs twice.
2. Code, commands, paths, numbers, errors are the payload. One changed character breaks them.
3. Ceremony is expensive, grammar is cheap. "Sure, I'd be happy to help" is ten tokens. "the" is one.
4. A dropped negation costs more than every token saved. Clarity beats compression.

## Rules

### 1. Answer first

Answer, then reason, then next step. Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Bad: "Sure! I'd be happy to help. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Good: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

### 2. Kill ceremony

No greeting, hedging, pleasantries, recap, or closer. No "Sure!", "Let me", "I'll now", "Hope this helps". No just/really/basically/actually/simply.

### 3. Short word

"fix" not "implement a solution for". Standard acronyms fine (DB, API, HTTP). Invented abbreviations not (cfg, impl, fn): same tokens, harder read. No arrows.

### 4. Articles optional, meaning never

Drop a/an/the when the sentence still reads in one pass. Fragments fine. Never drop not/never/no/only/except. Numbers and units exact.

Bad: "Migration drop column backup first."
Good: "Back up first. Then run migration: it drops the column."

### 5. One idea per sentence

ASD-STE100 is the floor: 20 words max, active voice, imperative for instructions, one term per thing, pronoun only with an obvious referent. Compression and clarity conflict? Clarity wins.

### 6. Payload verbatim

Code blocks unchanged. Commands, paths, API names exact. Errors quoted exact, shortest decisive line only. Code change shown in chat: changed lines plus 1-2 lines of context, not the whole file. Whole file only if the user asks, the file is new, or most of it changes. Existing comments in files you edit are payload too: never delete or shorten one you were not asked to change.

### 7. Tool runs: bounded status

No text between routine calls. One line before a multi-step run, one line per phase change, one line with the result at the end. Otherwise text before a call only to clarify, warn, or disambiguate.

### 8. User's language

Compress the style, not the language. An explicit reply-language instruction wins. Never switch because of quoted text. Technical terms and errors stay verbatim. Particles and case markers are grammar, not filler.

### 9. Never perform caveman

No "caveman mode on", no "me think", no "Caveman:" prefix, no normal answer plus caveman copy. No decorative tables or emoji. Never add a word to sound caveman. Caveman phrasing not shorter than plain? Use plain.

## When to break the rules

Plain prose, then resume:

1. Security warning.
2. Irreversible action. Confirm in full sentences first.
3. Step order a fragment could scramble.
4. User confused or repeats the question.
5. Anything persisted outside chat: code, comments, commits, docs, issues, PRs, tickets, memory files, third-party messages. `/caveman-compress` exempt.
6. Harness asks for a status line or confirmation. Give it. Harness decides *when* you speak, caveman decides *how*.
7. You ask the user a question or offer options. Full sentences, so the answer comes back right first time.

## Pre-send check

1. First sentence announces what you will do? Delete.
2. Last sentence recaps or offers help? Delete.
3. Every not/never/no/only present? Every code span, path, number, error verbatim?
4. Any sentence with two readings? Make it a full sentence.

Switch: /caveman, /ultracave, /megacave. Off: "stop caveman" or "normal mode".

Surfaces employer policy warning once; jurisdiction/retention per spec §13.1. Uses the local mcp-transcribe MCP (Whisper file STT) when available. Not an agent—a skill orchestrating tools and track-application patterns. Also invocable via /career-navigator:interview-capture.

Sets up the job search folder, builds the user profile, ExperienceLibrary and application tracker from existing documents, walks through the Indeed MCP connector (browser OAuth) for live job search, optional Apify for salary data, optional Gmail / Microsoft 365 inbox and optional Google Calendar connectors (OAuth) for outreach and meeting context, optional LinkedIn post analytics, and optional cloud storage connectors (Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox) when applicable. No Customize button required — run this command to do everything.

- career-navigator:list-artifacts: Lists all generated artifacts in the artifact inventory with metadata: type, date created, target role and company, ATS score if available, and linked application outcome if known. Fires when the user asks to see their generated documents or artifact history. Also invocable via /career-navigator:list-artifacts.
- career-navigator:market-brief: Generates a market intelligence brief for the user's target roles, including role demand trends, AI/automation displacement signals, and geographic competitiveness context. Invokes the market-researcher agent.

- career-navigator:mock-interview: Starts a mock interview session with configurable mode (guided, random, adaptive), stage (recruiter, hiring manager, technical, panel, executive, final), and vibe (supportive through bored). If mode or vibe are omitted, the system selects defaults and announces them. Delegates to interview-coach. Text-only. Also invocable via /career-navigator:mock-interview.
- career-navigator:negotiate-offer: Produces negotiation leverage and a send-ready negotiation draft via writer. Loads OfferContext persisted by evaluate-offer and avoids re-collecting already-known details.
- career-navigator:network-map: Maps plausible paths and gaps from the user to target employers—bridges, hypotheses, and dream-job leverage points. Outputs prose plus network_map_v1 JSON for a future visualization layer. Invokes networking-strategist.
- career-navigator:networking-strategy: Builds an evidence-based networking plan for target roles—priorities, sequencing, warm paths, and gap fixes. Outreach copy is handled by writer. Invokes networking-strategist.
- career-navigator:pattern-analysis: Analyzes application outcome data to find what's working and what isn't. Cross-references tracker history with artifact performance to update ExperienceLibrary weights and surface search_performance signals. Invokes the analyst agent.
- career-navigator:pipeline-status: Generates the Career Navigator pipeline status page: a filterable, collapsible table of every active application, focus/recommended role, closed outcome, and passed-on role, with an embedded application timeline. - career-navigator:prep-interview: Full interview preparation for a specific application or role: company and news context, stage-specific questions (recruiter, hiring manager, technical, panel, executive, final), and story evidence retrieved from StoryCorpus (with ExperienceLibrary fallback). Also invocable via /career-navigator:prep-interview.

Fires when compensation is mentioned in any context — offer evaluation, role targeting, or explicit request.

Mostly right. Three fixes.

- **Step 1 is bigger.** Reading includes unpacking attachments to text, and the LLM transcribing photos and scans. Without that, step 2 sees only the body.
- **Step 3 checks belong to code, not the LLM.** An LLM checking its own answer repeats its own mistake, costs tokens, and varies run to run. Code checks are exact and free: qty appears in `raw`, `raw` appears in the source, a request with zero lines gets `needs_review`. If "exist" means "exists in the catalog", that is the optional matcher, not the core.
- **Step 4: "it" is code, and caching is not a last step.** Duplicates and `revises` run after all emails, in code only. The cache wraps every LLM call from the first one. Otherwise the run without an API key fails.

Corrected order:

1. Code: read email, unpack attachments.
2. LLM: transcribe images and scans.
3. LLM: classify the email and extract the lines.
4. Code: check the lines.
5. Code: link revisions and mark duplicates across the inbox.
6. Code: write `parsed.json` and the cost report.

The cache sits under steps 2 and 3.

content.text:
Helper does MIME unpack only, and does it right. All 24 emails parse with zero MIME defects. All 15 attachments come out with bytes matching their extension.

Per email it gives: `id`, 8 `headers`, `text`, `html`, and `attachments[]` with `filename`, `mime`, `size`, `inline`, `content_id`, `path`.

**What it gets right**
- Pasted images are flagged `inline: true`, and the body keeps `[cid:image002.png]` at the paste spot (E010).
- The bounce's original message is saved as a separate `.eml`, not mixed into `text` (E013).
- `in_reply_to` links E004 to E003.

**What it leaves to us**
- **Attachments stay as bytes.** It never opens the xlsx, docx, PDF or image.
- **No split of current message from quoted history.** `text` is one string. E004, E011 and E020 quote with `>`. E012 and E016 use an Outlook block with no `>`.
- **Useful headers are dropped.** `Auto-Submitted: auto-replied` and `X-Failed-Recipients` (E013), `List-Unsubscribe` and `Precedence: bulk` (E014) identify the bounce and the newsletter without the LLM.
- **Thread headers are weak.** Only E004 and E020 have `In-Reply-To`. E011 and E012 are replies with none. E020 points to a message not in the inbox.
- **No error handling per email.** Directory mode is one dict comprehension, so one bad `.eml` kills the run. Bad base64 gives bytes with no error, so breakage shows only when opening the file.
- **Plain-text copy of an HTML table loses structure.** E024 `text` flattens the table to spaces; `html` keeps the spanning header. E018 has no `html` and puts one cell per line.
- **`date` is a raw string.** It needs parsing for the duplicate rule. All 24 parse.

**One fact confirmed:** the E006 and E008 PDFs are byte-identical (sha `6bb112499d`) while the bodies differ. Attachment hash is the duplicate signal, not body text.

Port the helper, do not use it as is: keep its logic, add the extra headers, an attachment hash, and a try/except per email.

"""MIME layer: turn .eml files into plain dicts, using data/eml_to_json.py.

This layer only unpacks the email. It does not open attachments and it does not
decide anything about the email's meaning.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import importlib.util
from pathlib import Path

_HELPER_PATH = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "data" / "eml_to_json.py"


def _load_eml_to_json():
    """Load the provided helper by file path, because data/ is not a package."""
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("eml_to_json", _HELPER_PATH)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module.eml_to_json


class MimeParser:
    """Parse every .eml in a directory. One bad email never stops the others."""

    def __init__(self, files_dir: Path | None = None):
        # Attachment bytes are written under files_dir/<email id>/<filename>.
        # With None, only attachment metadata is returned and nothing is written.
        self.files_dir = Path(files_dir) if files_dir else None
        self._eml_to_json = _load_eml_to_json()

    def parse_file(self, path: Path) -> dict:
        """Return one email as a dict. `error` is None unless the email could not be read."""
        path = Path(path)
        try:
            return {**self._eml_to_json(path, self.files_dir), "error": None}
        except Exception as exc:  # a broken .eml is recorded, not raised
            return {
                "id": path.stem,
                "headers": {},
                "text": None,
                "html": None,
                "attachments": [],
                "error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
            }

    def parse_dir(self, emails_dir: Path) -> dict[str, dict]:
        """Return every .eml in the directory, keyed by filename stem, in name order."""
        return {p.stem: self.parse_file(p) for p in sorted(Path(emails_dir).glob("*.eml"))}

from .eml_to_json import eml_to_json

That is a normal import and works from any folder and after install. The README allows it ("Use it, port it, or ignore it"). Cost: two copies of the file, since `data/eml_to_json.py` stays as shipped.
